findings.claim: Practice question 6 is typed '8 marks — Discuss' ("Discuss the benefits of using computational thinking techniques when developing a large software project.").
findings.truth: An impossible tariff on this paper. Topics 2.1 to 2.5 sit on the computational thinking, algorithms and programming component, which is 1 hour 30 minutes and 80 marks, split into a 50-mark concepts section and a 30-mark practical programming section, and whose paper 'will consist of short and medium answer questions'. The single 8-mark extended response question belongs to the other written component. The question itself is good practice, so only the tariff changes: 6 marks is the top of the range on this paper.
findings.evidence: Spec 3a, forms of assessment, both components; spec 2c places 2.1 to 2.5 in this component; spec content overview (non-calculator, two sections, all questions mandatory).

findings.claim: Practice question 6 is typed '8 marks — Extended Response' ("Compare pseudocode and flowcharts as tools for designing algorithms…").
findings.truth: The same impossible tariff as F1, and 'extended response' names a question type that only the other component carries. The task set is a comparison, so the type becomes '6 marks — Compare', which is already a house type in this unit (lesson 4 question 6).
findings.evidence: Spec 3a, forms of assessment; spec 2c topic placement.

findings.claim: Practice question 6 is typed '8 marks — Discuss' ("Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of a linear search and a binary search…").
findings.truth: The same impossible tariff as F1. Re-tariff to 6 marks and keep the command word.
findings.evidence: Spec 3a, forms of assessment; spec 2c topic placement.

findings.claim: The opening sentence defines the term with data-def="A precise sequence of steps that solves a problem or completes a task." on <dfn>searching algorithm</dfn>.
findings.truth: That is the definition of 'algorithm', copied from lesson 1, not of 'searching algorithm'. A student who taps the glossary term is shown a definition that says nothing about searching, even though the sentence around it gives the right meaning. The definition should name the search: a set of steps for finding a particular item of data inside a list or collection.
findings.evidence: Internal comparison with lesson 1 (glossary term 'Algorithm' carries the identical wording); spec 2.1.3 standard searching algorithms.

findings.claim: glossary_terms[0]: {"term": "searching algorithm", "definition": "A precise sequence of steps that solves a problem or completes a task."}
findings.truth: The same copied definition as F4, in the glossary list. Both fields must carry the corrected definition or the popup and the glossary disagree.

findings.claim: If you are asked to write code, use clear names and neat indentation, because marks are given for readable, well-structured solutions as well as for correct logic.
findings.truth: An invented mark-scheme claim. Nothing in the specification says that a written or refined program earns marks for readability on top of correct logic. Naming, indentation and commenting are examinable knowledge under maintainability (2.3.1); they are not a stated marking rule for programming answers. The advice itself is sound and should be given as advice.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented mark-scheme claims. Spec 3a describes this paper only as short and medium answer questions; spec 3b sets out how answers may be presented, not how they are credited.

findings.claim: Question 4 mark scheme: "Secure: pseudocode stores the opened file in a variable … for example open("scores.txt") then myFile.writeLine("Pass") then myFile.close()."
findings.truth: The model answer contradicts its own criterion and would not earn the first mark: it never assigns the opened file to myFile, yet the next two lines call methods on myFile. The lesson's own worked example writes myFile = open("sample.txt"), and the Exam Reference Language opens a file by assignment. The example needs the assignment restored.
findings.evidence: Recomputation against the same lesson's file-handling code block; spec 2.2.3 basic file handling operations (open, read, write, close).

findings.claim: The mark most often lost is confusing invalid with erroneous:
findings.truth: An unevidenced examiner-report claim. No published source ranks this as the most commonly lost mark. The warning is worth keeping, stated as a common mistake rather than as examiner data.
findings.evidence: House rule: no invented examiner claims. Spec 2.3.2 defines invalid and erroneous test data but says nothing about how often either is confused.

findings.claim: Seven lessons carry a sixth practice question typed '6 marks — Extended response' or '6 marks — Extended Response' (lessons 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10 and 11).
findings.truth: The tariff is possible, so these are not wrong in the way F1 to F3 are, but 'extended response' is the question type of the other written component; this paper is short and medium answer questions only. Options: (a) relabel to a command-word type in this unit alone (Discuss / Compare / Explain, matching each task); (b) relabel across the whole OCR computer-science subject, since the sibling unit computer-science/computer-systems sits on the component that really does carry an extended response and must keep the label; (c) leave it, because 'Extended Response' is a fleet-wide house label rather than a claim about the board's own naming. RECOMMEND (a): only this component's questions are mislabelled, the fix is one string per question, and it keeps the label honest for the sibling unit. Fold it into the question-type relabel sweep rather than editing here.
findings.evidence: Spec 3a, forms of assessment for both components; type strings counted in scripts/_retrofc/units/computer-science__computational-thinking/_raw.json (7 occurrences).
findings.ruling: NOTE: '6 marks - Extended response' labels on the J277/02 unit left for the question-type relabel sweep (relabel to the command word in this unit only; the /01 sibling genuinely carries an extended response).

findings.claim: function squared(number) / squared = number^2 / return squared / endfunction
findings.truth: The function assigns to a local variable with the same name as the function itself. The maths is right (squared(4) returns 16) and the code would run in the languages a student is likely to use, so no marks are at risk, but it models a habit that reads as if the function name were being reassigned. Not edited: the result is correct and rewriting a code block risks more than it fixes.
findings.evidence: Hand trace: 4^2 = 16; comparison with the Exam Reference Language function form (function … return … endfunction).

findings.claim: age >= 13 AND agreed == true (lesson 5) and student.feesPaid = true (lesson 6), while the prose and the lesson 6 glossary both write the Boolean values as True and False.
findings.truth: The Exam Reference Language writes the Boolean literals as True and False, so the code blocks disagree with the prose beside them. Not edited: the casing costs no marks (Section A accepts any clear presentation, and lower-case true is correct in several high-level languages a student may answer in), and both code blocks are otherwise valid. Worth folding into a subject-level code-style pass.
findings.evidence: Spec 3b, all code in examination papers is presented in the Exam Reference Language; internal comparison with the lesson 6 Boolean glossary entry.

summary: Every algorithm, trace and table in this unit recomputes correctly: the lesson 2 trace of total 0-3-8-10; the lesson 3 linear searches (45 found in 4 comparisons, 15 not found in 6) and the binary search of 2, 5, 8, 12, 16, 23, 38, 45, 56, 72, 91 for 45 (midpoints 23, 56, 38, 45; round-down convention applied consistently; 4 comparisons against 8 for a linear search); the 1,000-item counts (1,000 against about 10); the lesson 4 bubble sort of 5, 1, 4, 2 pass by pass, the insertion sort of 3, 7, 4, 1 with the correct shift-and-insert behaviour, the merge sort of 6, 2, 7, 1, and the practice bubble sort of 8, 3, 5, 1 (3, 5, 1, 8 then 3, 1, 5, 8 then 1, 3, 5, 8); every MOD, DIV and exponent result (17 DIV 5 = 3, 17 MOD 5 = 2, 3^2 = 9, 23 DIV 4 = 5, 23 MOD 4 = 3); all of lesson 10's truth tables, including all eight rows of Q = (A AND B) OR C and the worked Q = (A OR B) AND C for A = 1, B = 0, C = 1; and the lesson 9 test plan for the range 7 to 11. All 55 knowledge-check keys are correct, including all eleven match orders. No gate outside AND, OR and NOT is taught, the compiler and interpreter properties are the right way round, and the Exam Reference Language forms (if/elseif/endif, for/next, while/endwhile, procedure/endprocedure, function/return/endfunction, array declarations, open/readLine/writeLine/endOfFile/close) all match the board's own syntax. The defects are in the exam layer: three practice questions carry an 8-mark tariff that this paper cannot set, two invented examiner or mark-scheme claims, one glossary definition copied from the wrong term, and one file-handling model answer that omits the assignment its own criterion demands. Lessons 5, 6, 8, 10 and 11 carry nothing beyond the shared question-type label in F9.
